A Comprehensive Survey on Semantic Communication in Non-Terrestrial Networks: Architectures, Methodologies, and ChallengesThanks: Loc X. Nguyen, Avi Deb Raha, Huy Q. Le, Eui-Nam Huh, and Choong Seon Hong are with the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Kyung Hee University, Yongin-si, Gyeonggi-do 17104, Rep. of Korea, e-mails:{xuanloc088, avi, quanghuy69, johnhuh, cshong}@khu.ac.kr.Thanks: Zhu Han is with the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Houston, Houston, TX 77004 USA, and also with the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Kyung Hee University, Seoul, South Korea, 446-701. email:{hanzhu22}@gmail.com.

Loc X. Nguyen    Avi Deb Raha    Huy Q. Le    Zhu Han Affiliation: Eui-Nam Huh , and Choong Seon Hong 
Abstract

The sixth-generation wireless networks are envisioned to deliver ubiquitous, seamless, and intelligent connectivity that reaches far beyond the limits of terrestrial infrastructure. Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) are central to this vision, extending coverage to underserved regions, remote terrain, and disaster zones that terrestrial deployment cannot economically reach. However, NTN architecture faces numerous limitations: severe path loss over long distances, long propagation delays, large and time-varying Doppler shifts, limited visibility windows, and tight on-board energy and computing budgets. Semantic communication (SemCom), which conveys the meaning of data rather than its raw bit-level representation, is unusually well matched to these conditions: extreme compression rate for task-oriented eases bandwidth scarcity, deep joint source-channel coding prevents the cliff effect due to low signal-to-noise ratio, and generative-AI reconstructs content from sparse cues that survive rain-faded or blocked links. This observation, that each NTN limitation maps onto a SemCom property that addresses it, motivates our survey. We first walk through the NTN limitations one by one, pairing each with the SemCom design choices that complement it, then we organize the literature along three axes: the NTN platform, the semantic methodology, and the supporting techniques, and follow this with platform-by-platform deep dives on satellite-centric, UAV/HAPS-centric, and integrated SAGIN systems. The survey concludes by identifying open research problems, gaps in existing standards, and future directions, including the application of foundation models, energy-aware scheduling, and quantum-assisted SemCom for deep space communication.

Index Terms: 
Semantic communication, Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs), 6G, space-air-ground integrated networks (SAGINs), low Earth orbit (LEO) satellites, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), high-altitude platform stations (HAPS), deep joint source-channel coding (D-JSCC), Generative AI, Theory-of-Mind.

I Introduction

The rapid growth of connected devices, immersive applications, and latency-sensitive services is pushing terrestrial wireless networks to their operational limits [1]. Non-terrestrial networks (NTNs) have emerged as a key component in 6G, not only to address these limitations but also to provide seamless connectivity in rural areas, where installing new terrestrial infrastructure is extremely expensive [2, 3, 4, 5]. NTNs consist of satellites, high-altitude platform stations (HAPS), unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and ships. Together, they cover large areas to provide global coverage and flexible services. However, NTNs face major communication challenges, such as severe path loss, long delays, Doppler shifts, intermittent connections, atmospheric attenuation, and limited onboard resources [6, 7]. These issues make traditional bit-level communication less efficient for NTN systems.

Semantic communication (SemCom) changes the goal from delivering every bit reliably to making sure the meaning is understood [8]. By sending only the information needed for the task, using AI to encode and reconstruct messages, SemCom can greatly reduce communication overhead while still supporting task performance. In addition, SemCom has demonstrated substantial gains in compression efficiency, channel robustness under harsh environments, bandwidth, and power-constrained wireless environments over the conventional bit communication [9, 10, 11]. These advantages make SemCom a highly promising paradigm for future NTN and SAGIN architectures, which motivates a number of works [12, 13, 14, 15] to study this integration. The current works on SemCom can be divided into three categories: 1) Deep Joint Source-Channel Coding (D-JSCC), 2) Theory of Mind, and, most recently, 3) Generative AI. Each direction is built on a different theoretical foundation and thus has unique definitions of data semantics and ways of presenting and interpreting data.

I-A Scope, Contributions, and Distinction from Other Surveys

Despite the rapid growth of research on semantic communication in NTNs, there are limited works that have dedicated surveys that provide a systematic review of this emerging area. Specifically, the work [24] was the first survey to provide a literature review of SemCom in NTNs, where they mainly focus on the deep joint source-channel coding works for SemCom. The theory-of-mind direction is only briefly discussed and completely overlooks the generative AI direction, which we comprehensively cover in our survey. While the existing SemCom surveys mainly focused on a specific direction or subjects: [11] tried to convince that the Theory-of-Mind direction is the correct way to conduct SemCom, [17] focused on the architecture, security, and privacy of D-JSCC and Theory-of-Mind. Similarly, the survey [25] reviews the literature with resource management, security, and privacy issues. [26] divided SemCom works into semantic-oriented communication, goal-oriented communication, and semantic-awareness communication, [27] studied the metrics for SemCom. On the other hand [28, 29] mainly discussed the techniques, applications, and future challenges, [30] presented a useful tutorial-cum-survey to explain why we need SemCom.

In the meantime, surveys on NTN architectures and networking technologies limit their discussion to hardware improvements, the multiple-input multiple-output technique, and resource optimization  [31, 32, 33]. Only a handful of recent works have begun to provide short discussions about the complement of two paradigms: [13] provided an early vision on SC-based NTN architectures, [24] surveyed semantic communications in space-air-ground-sea integrated networks (SAGSIN) with a focus on the D-JSCC, and [18, 22] discussed generative AI for SAGIN. However, none of these provides a unified review that simultaneously (a) explains the necessary background on both NTN and SemCom, (b) walks the reader through every NTN limitation and the SemCom design choice that addresses it, (c) systematically organizes the literature along the platform, methodology, and supporting-technique axes, and (d) provides side-by-side comparisons of representative works. In Table I, we provide a comparison of our survey against existing surveys. The main contributions of this survey can be summarized as follows:

  • •

    We first provide a detailed limitation-by-limitation discussion of how SemCom addresses the fundamental limitations of NTN, including severe path loss, long propagation delay, Doppler shift, intermittent connectivity, atmospheric attenuation, on-board SWaP-C constraints, and multi-hop distortion accumulation. Rather than treating them as a set of impairments, we pair each limitation with the SemCom property that complements it.

  • •

    We consider a three-axis taxonomy spanning: the NTN platform, the semantic methodology, and the supporting technique, to systematically classify and discuss representative works, while delivering platform-by-platform deep dives on (i) satellite-centric SemCom, (ii) UAV-centric SemCom, and (iii) integrated SAGIN/SAGSIN SemCom. For each platform, we examine how its distinctive constraints, and shape the corresponding SemCom design,

  • •

    We provide summary tables that map representative works to their data modality, semantic method, channel and protocol considerations, supporting techniques, and target metrics. Together with a comparison against existing surveys, these tables give a structured overview of the design space, highlight well-studied and open directions, and serve as a practical reference for future work.

  • •

    We highlight key open challenges, including on-board model compression, high-Doppler channel adaptation, knowledge-base alignment, energy-aware semantic scheduling, and SemCom security. For each challenge, we identify the main blocker and the NTN platform most affected. Finally, we discuss future directions such as foundation-model-based SemCom and quantum-assisted semantic transmission for deep-space networks.

I-B Structure of the Survey

The remainder of the survey is organized as in Fig. 1. Section II provides background on NTN architecture and semantic communication. Section III is the motivation of the survey, where it walks through each NTN limitation and explains, with examples and references, how semantic communication addresses it. Section IV introduces a generic four-layer architectural framework for SemCom over NTN. Sections V, VI, and VII provide platform-specific deep dives on satellite, UAV, and integrated SAGIN/SAGSIN systems, respectively. Section VIII identifies open challenges and outlines future directions. Section IX concludes.

II Background and Fundamentals

This section provides a brief overview of the foundations for the rest of the paper: the architecture of NTNs, the building blocks of satellite communication (SATCOM), and the principles of semantic communication. Specifically, Sections II-A and II-B recall the features of NTNs and their communication fundamentals, while Section II-C then introduces a comprehensive knowledge of the three main SemCom directions. Fig. 2 provides a unified view of the NTN layers, their communication and networking aspects, and representative SemCom scenarios.

II-A Architecture of Non-Terrestrial Networks

To provide a complete overview, we briefly review the NTN architecture in the following sections. More detailed discussions can be found in [23, 34]. At the highest level, spaceborne nodes are divided into LEO (300300-2,0002{,}000 km), MEO (2,0002{,}000-35,78635{,}786 km), and GEO (∼\sim35,78635{,}786 km) tiers. These tiers balance factors such as propagation delay (ranging from a few milliseconds to about 700700 ms round-trip), visibility window (55-1515 minutes per LEO pass compared to continuous GEO coverage), and Doppler effects with compute, energy, and antenna constraints. Mega-constellations like Starlink address the limited visibility of single satellites by providing continuous overhead coverage [35, 36, 37, 38]. The atmospheric layers include HAPS at 1717-2525 km (which are quasi-stationary, with 0.10.1-11 ms round-trip [39, 40]) and UAVs that operate from ground level up to a few kilometers (these are trajectory-controllable and limited by size, weight, and power [41]). When these spaceborne, airborne, aerial, and terrestrial tiers are stitched together-possibly with maritime and underwater nodes-the result is a SAGIN or SAGSIN architecture [42] whose heterogeneous per-hop links and administrative boundaries are precisely where SemCom adds value: per-hop coding can adapt locally without re-decoding the underlying meaning, and the same semantic latent can flow across radio, optical inter-satellite, and acoustic underwater segments with only the channel codec changing. Three system-level features of modern NTN matter for the rest of this survey. (i) The conventional four-segment decomposition into space, ground, control/management, and user segments [43, 44, 45, 46] maps to four distinct opportunities for semantic processing: on-board near the raw sensor data, on the ground for heavy generative decoding, in the control plane for AI-driven orchestration, and at the user device for personalized reconstruction. (ii) The transition from transparent (bent-pipe) payloads to regenerative payloads with digital channelization, on-board beamforming, and software-defined modems [47] is the hardware substrate on which on-board SemCom can be deployed. (iii) The 3GPP standardization of NTN in Releases 17-18 [48, 49] and the anticipated AI/ML-native integration in Release 20 [34] raise the open question-revisited in Section VIII-of whether SemCom will eventually enter the standard as an application-layer service or as a native AI/ML feature.

II-B Communication Fundamentals in NTNs

We restrict the discussion to communication essentials in NTNs; readers are referred to [6] for full link-budget and waveform treatments. Three link-level properties define the operating envelope of any SemCom system over NTN: severe free-space path loss-exceeding 200200 dB at Ka-band GEO, with 55-2020 dB additional atmospheric margin for rain, gas absorption, and scintillation, often driving the working SNR below 00 dB during heavy fading [50, 51, 52, 53]; a time-varying channel with large Doppler and rapidly evolving SNR (1010-2020 dB swings across a single LEO pass); and a power-limited operating regime imposed by on-board solar, battery, and thermal constraints [54]. Each of these is precisely the regime in which bit-fidelity-centric design degrades sharply and the smooth distortion-SNR behaviour of SemCom becomes attractive (Section III). At the physical and access layers, modern high-throughput satellites generate dozens to hundreds of spot beams with digital beamforming and beam-hopping [55, 56, 57], managing adjacent-beam interference through frequency-and-polarization reuse and multi-user precoding [58, 59]. Flexible payloads further reconfigure per-beam power, bandwidth, beamwidth, pointing, and beam-hopping pattern in software [60, 61, 62, 63]-the same on-board DSP/SDR substrate that enables on-board SemCom. Classical FDMA/TDMA/CDMA is increasingly supplemented by next-generation multiple access (NGMA): SDMA [64], NOMA [65, 66, 67], and RSMA [68, 69, 70], each of which has been combined with semantic-aware resource allocation in the recent literature [20]. RSMA is particularly attractive for SemCom because the common stream can naturally carry the most semantically important content while private streams carry user-specific refinement. At the network layer, LEO mega-constellations are best viewed as in-orbit packet-switched networks connected by inter-satellite links (ISLs)-increasingly optical, with multi-Gb/s rates-that enable on-orbit collaboration, federated learning, and semantic-domain forwarding without re-encoding [71, 72]. Classical shortest-path routing over time-varying snapshot topologies [73, 74, 75] scales poorly to mega-constellations of thousands of satellites, which has driven a rapid migration to ML-based routing: CNNs for link-congestion prediction [76], recurrent networks for ISL traffic forecasting [77], deep Q-learning for joint routing/caching/computation across SAGIN [78], and multi-agent RL for bottleneck-aware route selection [79]. The same dynamic environment also drives classical resource allocation (per-beam power and bandwidth, beam-hopping pattern, user scheduling, gateway switching [80]) from convex methods and metaheuristics toward deep RL and federated/multi-agent control. As Section V will show, the routing and resource-allocation decisions that are optimal for bit rate are not necessarily optimal for semantic fidelity [81]-the central re-design challenge in NTN-SemCom.

II-C Semantic Communication: Principles and Paradigms

II-C1 From bit fidelity to semantics and effectiveness

Weaver, in his commentary on Shannon’s seminal paper [82, 8], identified three levels of communication: Level A (technical-how accurately bits are transmitted, the classical Shannon target), Level B (semantic-how precisely the transmitted symbols convey the desired meaning), and Level C (effectiveness-how effectively the received meaning affects conduct). Conventional SATCOM operates at Level A under a bit-fidelity-centric philosophy in which every bit is sacred. This becomes inefficient when the link is at low SNR, the contact window is short, on-board energy is scarce, or the receiver only cares about a downstream task-each of which is a defining characteristic of NTN, not an exception. SemCom elevates the design to Levels B and C (often called goal-oriented or task-oriented communication), allocating resources by semantic value rather than bit rate. For example, sending a 4-megapixel satellite image of a flooded area usually takes hundreds of kilobytes of compressed data. In contrast, a SemCom system could send just a segmentation mask, a brief caption like “flooded village near 43.6∘43.6^{\circ}N, 1.4∘1.4^{\circ}E”, or polygon coordinates of detected objects. This approach cuts the data size by a huge margin while still giving the rescue operator all the necessary information.

Although the underlying information-theoretic question predates Shannon-style channel coding, Carnap and Bar-Hillel proposed a theory of semantic information based on logical probability as early as 1952 [83], two obstacles delayed its practical adoption: semantic information has no universally accepted unit [84], and meaning depends jointly on source data, receiver task, and receiver prior knowledge. Learning-based SemCom reverses the order, building practical encoders and decoders first and proposing performance metrics suited to them [85, 86, 87].

II-C2 Architecture, system model, and source modalities

A defining feature of SemCom is the knowledge base (KB) shared and often jointly maintained by transmitter and receiver [88]. The KB encapsulates prior knowledge (geography, common-sense facts, vocabularies, foundation-model weights) and downstream-task awareness. In the canonical architecture [26], the transmitter performs semantic encoding (using Transformer [89], BERT [90], or foundation models with reference to the KB), channel encoding, and transmission; the receiver performs the reverse, with semantic decoding replacing classical source decoding. A canonical SemCom system can be written as the cascade

𝐬^=fdec​(h⁡(fenc​(𝐬,𝜽e))+𝐧,𝜽d),\hat{\mathbf{s}}=f_{\text{dec}}\!\big(\,h(f_{\text{enc}}(\mathbf{s};\boldsymbol{\theta}_{e}))+\mathbf{n};\,\boldsymbol{\theta}_{d}\,\big), (1)

trained end-to-end under a power constraint 1k​𝔼​[‖x‖2]≤P\frac{1}{k}\mathbb{E}[\|x\|^{2}]\leq P. For reconstruction-oriented SemCom, the objective is

min𝜽e,𝜽d⁡𝔼s,h,n​[dsem​(s,s^)]+λ​R​(𝜽e),\min_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{e},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{d}}\;\mathbb{E}_{s,h,n}\!\left[d_{\text{sem}}(s,\hat{s})\right]+\lambda\,R(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{e}), (2)

here, dsemd_{\text{sem}} measures semantic distortion (such as pixel-wise MSE, perceptual loss, or BERT cosine for text), and RR is a regularization term for bandwidth, latency, or model size. In goal-oriented SemCom, the focus moves from data accuracy to how well the task is performed:

max𝜽e,𝜽d⁡𝔼s,h,n​[U⁡(𝒯⁡(s^),ytask)]−μ​𝔼​[C⁡(𝜽e,𝜽d)],\max_{\boldsymbol{\theta}_{e},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{d}}\;\mathbb{E}_{s,h,n}\!\left[U\!\left(\mathcal{T}(\hat{s}),\,y_{\text{task}}\right)\right]-\mu\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[C(\boldsymbol{\theta}_{e},\boldsymbol{\theta}_{d})\right], (3)

where 𝒯⁡(⋅)\mathcal{T}(\cdot) maps the reconstruction to a task output, UU is a task utility (accuracy, mission success), and CC is the on-board computation cost, which is especially relevant in NTN. SemCom designs to date concentrate on three principal modalities. Text is the most studied: early LSTM designs [91, 92] have given way to Transformer-based encoders such as DeepSC [89] that are robust at low SNR-a natural fit for telemetry, situation reports, and news broadcast over NTN. Image SemCom typically uses CNN- or ViT-based features and is the modality most studied in NTN because of its alignment with Earth-observation imagery [93, 94, 95]; in task-oriented designs, only the task output is required at the receiver. Speech introduces variable rate, prosody, dialect, and emotion that pure text-level transcription discards [96]; early CNN-based designs have given way to self-supervised speech foundation models such as wav2vec 2.0 [97] and HuBERT [98, 99]. SATCOM-specific speech SemCom remains thin, but the use case-voice connectivity for maritime crews, polar expeditions, aviation, and disaster response is precisely where NTN delivers unique value. Multimodal SemCom jointly encoding audio, video, and text is emerging and well-suited to NTN broadcast services [100].

II-C3 Three SemCom paradigms

We adopt the three-direction categorization of [101]. The paradigms differ in (i) what semantic representation is transmitted and (ii) how the receiver reconstructs, or acts on it. A simple example of a fundamental difference among approaches is presented in Fig. 3.

In the first direction, Theory-of-Mind or Knowledge Graph Semantic Communication [102], both the transmitter and receiver share a knowledge base 𝒦\mathcal{K} and only exchange structured semantic content that the listener cannot already infer. The source is represented as a semantic graph G=⟨E,R⟩G=\langle E,R\rangle made up of (head, relation, tail) triplets. Only the new subset Δ​G={ϕ∈G:ϕ∉𝒦R​x}\Delta G=\{\phi\in G:\phi\notin\mathcal{K}_{Rx}\} is sent, while a reasoning operator Π\Pi at the receiver fills in any missing or partial triplets using context and the shared knowledge base. This approach compresses data in two ways: it uses graph-based abstraction to replace complex raw data with a few symbolic triplets, and it allows the speaker to skip information that the listener can recover from the knowledge base. Possible extensions include hierarchical belief sets for goal-oriented teamwork, causal-structure models, and systems where the symbolic vocabulary is learned through interaction between speaker and listener. For NTN, this method is especially useful because synchronizing the knowledge base between speaker and listener can be spread out over the many short visibility periods of an LEO pass. Also, graph-structured semantics are naturally robust to channel noise, since corrupted entities can often be reconstructed from related information using Π\Pi.

In the second direction, Generative-AI-based Semantic Communication, a generative model GϕG_{\phi}-such as a diffusion model, large language model, or vision-language foundation model-serves as the decoder. The transmitter sends only a small prompt or latent p=fextract​(s,θp)p=f_{\text{extract}}(s;\theta_{p}), which is much smaller than the original source ss. The receiver then samples the reconstruction s^∼Gϕ(⋅∣p^,ξ)\hat{s}\sim G_{\phi}(\cdot\mid\hat{p},\xi) instead of computing it in a fixed way. For diffusion decoders, this means gradually denoising an initial Gaussian sample using a learned noise predictor based on p^\hat{p}. The training goal combines accuracy, perceptual quality, and distributional similarity (such as LPIPS, KL, or adversarial losses). Since GϕG_{\phi} has strong built-in knowledge of natural data, the prompt |p||p| can be extremely small-sometimes just a few tokens. This makes the approach especially suitable for the rain-faded Ka-band conditions discussed in Section III.

In the third direction, D-JSCC uses a single neural network to handle both source compression and channel coding. It maps the source directly to channel symbols x=fθ​(s):ℝd→ℂkx=f_{\theta}(s):\mathbb{R}^{d}\!\to\!\mathbb{C}^{k}, with a bandwidth-compression ratio ρ=k/d\rho=k/d, and the output is decoded end-to-end by gϕg_{\phi} as described in (2). The main advantage of D-JSCC, and the reason it is widely used in satellite imagery, is its smooth distortion-to-SNR curve. This avoids the sudden quality drop, or cliff effect, that happens with traditional separate source and channel coding near the SNR threshold. A digital version, D2-JSCC [103], adds vector quantization to work with standard waveforms like DVB-S2X and NR-NTN. D-JSCC is preferred for satellite imagery because the channel SNR can change by 10-20 dB during a single LEO pass, the data is high-dimensional and suitable for neural compression, and it avoids cliff effects during deep fades.

III Limitations of Non-Terrestrial Networks and How Semantic Communication Complements Them

NTN links systematically penalize bit-fidelity-centric design. We group the limitations into four categories-adverse channel conditions, time constraints, platform constraints, and distributed heterogeneous data-and identify, for each, the SemCom mechanisms that turn them into design opportunities. Table II summarizes the mapping.

III-A Adverse Channel Conditions: Path Loss, Doppler, and Atmospherics

Free-space path loss is over 200 dB at Ka-band GEO and reaches 230-250 dB on interplanetary links. Rain, gas absorption, and ionospheric scintillation add another 5-20 dB [121]. An LEO satellite traveling at about 7.5 km/s causes Doppler shifts ranging from tens to hundreds of kHz at S/Ka-band. According to the small-offset approximation in [122], the Doppler shift and the resulting OFDM inter-carrier interference are given by:

fd=vrelc​fc​cos⁡ϑ,ICI≈π23​(fdΔ​f)2.f_{d}=\frac{v_{\text{rel}}}{c}\,f_{c}\,\cos\vartheta,\qquad\mathrm{ICI}\approx\frac{\pi^{2}}{3}\left(\frac{f_{d}}{\Delta f}\right)^{2}. (4)

Here, vrelv_{\text{rel}} is the relative velocity, ϑ\vartheta is the angle between the line of sight and velocity (so fdf_{d} changes sign during a pass), and Δ​f\Delta f is the OFDM subcarrier spacing. ϑ\vartheta is used instead of θ\theta to avoid confusion with encoder and decoder parameters in Section II-C. When using separate source and channel coding, the low and changing SNR can cause the cliff effect, and GNSS-aided pre-compensation often leaves residual errors that do not work well with high-order modulation. SemCom helps in these situations by using D-JSCC’s smooth distortion-SNR curve [123], channel-adaptive codecs like Cao et al.’s channel code-book [109], and importance-aware methods such as IRST [94]. It also uses aggressive task-oriented compression, for example, sending just a single bit to indicate wildfire presence instead of a full image [105]. Other approaches include generative regeneration from sparse cues (FMSAT [93]), foundation-model decoders that can handle residual symbol errors if the main meaning is preserved [124], semantic-cue-driven Doppler estimation as a feedback loop [125], and weather-aware mode switching that uses 30-120 seconds of nowcasting to re-route through site diversity or pre-buffer important content [100, 112, 126]. Another interesting SemCom approach was introduced in [127] to handle changes in data distribution with online learning.

III-B Time Constraints: Propagation Delay and Short Visibility Windows

Round-trip delays of 5-12 ms for LEO [128], 100-250 ms for MEO, 500-700 ms for GEO, and 4-22 minutes for Earth-Mars are hard physical limits, and LEO passes last only 5-15 minutes (Fig. 4). HARQ and adaptive coding become stale before feedback arrives, closed-loop control of remote actuators is infeasible, and bulk transfer is constrained by window length. SemCom does not shorten delay but transmits actionable information directly-e.g., “vehicle detected at (x,y)(x,y), confidence 0.92” rather than raw telemetry [106, 105, 107]-and enables semantic-aware delay/disruption-tolerant networking, where Bundle Protocol and Contact Graph Routing prioritize content by relevance rather than arrival order [108]. For short contacts, drastic 10-100×\times compression [95], knowledge-base-driven delta encoding from shared knowledge graphs [129, 130, 100], and semantic/version-AoI scheduling that prioritizes the freshest important updates [110] convert scarce link time into useful task throughput. The design shifts from “transmit everything and decide later” to “decide first, transmit only what matters.”

III-C Platform Constraints: SWaP-C and Multi-Hop Topology

Small LEO satellites have power limits of just tens to hundreds of watts, and their radiation-hardened FPGAs or ASICs are about ten years behind ground-based GPUs. UAVs must also balance computation with flight time. If a SemCom system uses more energy for extracting semantics than it saves during transmission, the overall benefit is lost [106]. This creates a trade-off [106, 114].

Etotal​(ρ)\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{total}}(\rho) =Eenc​(ρ)⏟on-board+k⁡(ρ)B​P⏟transmission,\displaystyle=\underbrace{E_{\mathrm{enc}}(\rho)}_{\text{on-board}}+\underbrace{\frac{k(\rho)}{B}P}_{\text{transmission}}, (5)
ρ⋆\displaystyle\rho^{\star} =arg⁡minρ​Etotal​(ρ)​s.t.​Q​(ρ)≥Qmin,\displaystyle=\arg\min_{\rho}\,E_{\mathrm{total}}(\rho)\;\;\text{s.t.}\;\;Q(\rho)\geq Q_{\min}, (6)

A smaller compression ratio ρ\rho means fewer transmitted symbols k⁡(ρ)k(\rho), but it increases the encoder’s energy use Eenc​(ρ)E_{\mathrm{enc}}(\rho), as long as the task quality stays above QminQ_{\min}. Because of this, NTN-SemCom systems need to be both asymmetric and modular. Lightweight on-board encoders, such as sparse compressed-learning matrices [113] or distilled models, work together with more powerful ground-based generative decoders. Energy-aware mode switching lets the system choose between bit-level and SemCom modes using DRL [112]. Heavy semantic processing can also be offloaded to HAPS or other satellites [114]. The multi-hop NTN path (user →\to UAV/LEO →\to ISL →\to gateway →\to backhaul) can add distortion in regenerative pipelines or noise in transparent ones [115]. This is managed by per-hop semantic denoising trained with the codec [115], semantic-forward relaying [116], codebook-domain forwarding that avoids full re-encoding [117], and joint semantic coding-and-routing that aims to maximize end-to-end semantic fidelity instead of just per-hop bit rate (GraphJSCR [81]).

III-D Distributed Heterogeneous Data

Each satellite or UAV gathers a different area, time frame, or type of data. Pooling all this data in one place is not practical because of downlink limits and privacy or sovereignty concerns. Federated learning fits well with the layered NTN setup. For example, SemSpaceFL [104] aggregates data first at ground gateways and then at a global cloud server, using weights based on orbital and link features. NomaFedHAP [119] uses HAPS as parameter servers with NOMA-based exchanges. Semantic-aware task clustering [118] groups nodes in the semantic domain to prevent harmful cooperation between different tasks. Designs where HAPS act as FL servers with GEO/MEO relays [120] map aggregation directly onto the NTN layers.

III-E Summary: a Two-Way Reinforcement

NTNs are not just a promising area for semantic communication, but they also help drive its progress. The unique challenges of NTN environments, like fast-changing channels, unstable connections, multi-hop relays, and limited on-board resources, push SemCom systems past traditional communication methods. To work well in these settings, SemCom needs to be flexible, energy-efficient, distributed, and focused on specific tasks. This has led to new techniques such as semantic-aware routing, latent-domain forwarding, adaptive semantic scheduling, federated semantic learning, and generative reconstruction. Many of these advances are likely to impact future terrestrial 6G systems, not just NTNs. In this way, NTNs are both a tough testing ground and a key factor in turning semantic communication into a practical solution for next-generation wireless networks.

IV Architectural Frameworks for Semantic Communication in NTN

Before diving into platform-specific works, it is useful to lay out a generic architectural template that captures what most NTN-SemCom systems do, regardless of whether the platform is an LEO satellite or a UAV swarm. A typical SC-based NTN consists of four conceptual layers: (i) sensing and semantic extraction at the source node; (ii) on-board/edge semantic encoding and channel coding; (iii) multi-hop wireless transport (which may span ISLs, feeder links, and access links); (iv) receiver-side semantic decoding/regeneration with optional knowledge-base feedback, as shown in Fig. 5. This four-layer view appears, with various names and small variations, in nearly every NTN-SemCom paper [13, 24, 107, 106].

IV-A Layer 1: Sensing and Semantic Extraction

Spaceborne and aerial nodes are foremost sensors: they capture imagery (optical, hyper-spectral, SAR), telemetry, video streams, audio, or text. The first job of a SemCom system is to extract from this raw stream the part that is meaningful for the downstream task. Typical extractors include CNNs, ResNets, or vision transformers for image features; semantic-segmentation models such as SegGPT for pixel-level labels [93]; object detectors (Faster R-CNN, YOLO) for bounding boxes; knowledge-graph constructors that produce subject-predicate-object triplets [102]; and foundation models that produce multimodal embeddings or natural-language captions [107, 100].

The choice depends on the task. For Earth observation, segmentation masks or detection results are usually sufficient [95, 135, 106]. For UAV-based surveillance, knowledge-graph triplets yield extreme compression [102]. For audiovisual broadcast over satellites, multimodal embeddings or per-modality keyframes are appropriate [100].

IV-B Layer 2: Semantic Encoding, Quantization, and Channel Coding

Once features are extracted, they must be turned into transmittable channel symbols. This layer is where the three SemCom paradigms diverge:

  • •

    In D-JSCC, the same neural network produces channel-ready symbols directly, where they are analog signal [9].

  • •

    In digital SemCom (D2-JSCC), the encoder produces discrete symbols compatible with off-the-shelf modulation [103], possibly via a vector-quantized variational autoencoder (VQ-VAE), while the receiver uses the nearest neighbor look-up to decode the feature representation.

  • •

    In generative SemCom, the encoder produces extremely compact prompts or low-dimensional latent codes, which are then channel-coded with conventional codes since their volume is small [93, 100].

Beyond the choice of paradigm, several quantization-related design choices for NTN deployments. Analog D-JSCC creates real-valued channel symbols, so it needs a software-defined radio with high-resolution digital-to-analog conversion at the transmitter. This setup works for regenerative payloads, but it is difficult to use with older bent-pipe satellites that rely on standardized waveforms. Digital SemCom resolves this incompatibility by funneling the semantic latent through a vector quantizer [136] or a learned scalar quantizer) and then mapping the discrete codes to QAM/PSK symbols compatible with DVB-S2X, NR-NTN, or other standardized waveforms[103, 137, 138]. The resulting digital interface is essential when the transmitter and receiver are operated by different stakeholders or when the SemCom layer must coexist with bit-level traffic on the same satellite (e.g., NOMA-style superposition [139]). One important point is that the encoder, quantizer, and channel coder cannot be designed separately. Quantization noise and channel noise affect each other, so the encoder must consider both during training to prevent serious problems when the system is deployed.

IV-C Layer 3: Multi-Hop Wireless Transport

NTN links rarely consist of a single physical channel. A typical end-to-end path may include an access link from the user to a UAV or LEO satellite; one or more inter-satellite links (ISLs, often free-space optical) within a constellation; a feeder link from the satellite to a ground gateway; and a terrestrial backhaul. Each hop has its own SNR, Doppler, latency, and atmospheric conditions. A unique question for NTN-SemCom is how to relay semantic information across hops without re-decoding and re-encoding at each step, which both wastes energy and accumulates distortion [115, 116, 117].

IV-D Layer 4: Semantic Decoding, Regeneration, and Knowledge Update

At the receiver, the semantic codes-now affected by the channel-are processed by a decoder that does one of three things, depending on the application. It can fully reconstruct the original data, such as a high-resolution image. It can extract a task-specific result, like a segmentation mask, detection boxes, or a classification label. Or, in goal-oriented scenarios, it can directly produce an action or control signal. Generative decoders such as conditional diffusion models [140, 141, 142], conditional GANs [93], and large language models [100] can generate realistic content from limited codes. This is especially helpful when the connection is weak, since the decoder can fill in missing textures or complete occluded areas in a way that looks real and matches the sender’s intent. However, this requires significant computing power at the receiver, which is manageable at ground stations but challenging on satellites. The receiver can also update a shared knowledge base. For example, it might add a new building to a map, improve its understanding of the transmitter, or collect data for later review. These updates make future communication more efficient. Updates can be local, affecting only that receiver; reciprocal, where the receiver confirms the update so the transmitter knows what to skip next time; or global, where the update spreads through the network using FL aggregation [104, 143, 118]. The best method depends on the trust model, available resources for syncing knowledge bases, and how quickly the environment changes.

IV-E Common Performance Metrics

In SemCom, the importance of a message depends on what the receiver needs to do, so we cannot use a single standard metric like BER in Shannon-style coding. Instead, this survey covers seven groups of metrics that focus on fidelity, efficiency, and effectiveness.

  • •

    Pixel-level reconstruction: PSNR and MS-SSIM [9, 144] for image-level fidelity.

  • •

    Perceptual quality: learned perceptual image patch similarity (LPIPS) [145] and Fréchet inception distance (FID), which correlate with human judgment of generative outputs better than pixel-error measures.

  • •

    Text semantic similarity: BLEU, sentence similarity via cosine distance of BERT embeddings, and metric-of-semantic-similarity (MSS) [89], which-unlike BER-are insensitive to synonyms and rephrasing.

  • •

    Task accuracy: classification accuracy, object-detection mean average precision (mAP), and segmentation IoU [105, 102] for downstream-task fidelity.

  • •

    Bandwidth and compression: bandwidth-compression ratio (BCR), bits-per-pixel (BPP), and channel-symbols-per-source-symbol.

  • •

    Latency and freshness: end-to-end delay, age of information (AoI), version-AoI, query-AoI, and age of misclassified information (AoMI) [110, 111, 105].

  • •

    Goal/effectiveness metrics: task success probability and task-oriented semantic spectral efficiency (TOSSE) [94]; semantic transmission rate (S​-​RS\text{-}R) and semantic spectral efficiency (S​-​S​ES\text{-}SE), both expressed in semantic units (suts) [146]; and semantic energy efficiency (S​-​E​ES\text{-}EE, suts/J) [147], which is particularly relevant in NTN where on-board energy is the binding constraint.

Each group of metrics serves a different but important purpose. Reconstruction and perception metrics check how well the original source is kept. Task accuracy and goal metrics show how well the system meets its main goal. Bandwidth, latency, and energy-based metrics measure cost. The semantic-unit group (suts, S​-​S​ES\text{-}SE, S​-​E​ES\text{-}EE) is unique because it allows direct comparison between semantic and bit-level systems. Most NTN-SemCom evaluations use one fidelity or accuracy metric along with one cost-based metric, such as MS-SSIM with BCR or task accuracy with S​-​E​ES\text{-}EE, since focusing on only one side does not reveal the full trade-off.

Beyond evaluation, these metrics shape resource allocation, which in SemCom differs from classical SATCOM in three respects: (i) the objective often contains a non-differentiable, implicit semantic-similarity term that defeats standard convex methods [148]; (ii) the resource variables-the new semantic compression ratio [149] alongside transmit/receive compute, power, bandwidth, and beam pattern-are highly coupled and the resulting problem is non-convex [150], with the compression ratio simultaneously affecting extraction, transmission, and task-processing latencies in opposing directions; and (iii) allocation must follow semantic value rather than data volume, since not every feature is equally valuable [151]. Two solution families have emerged: centralized methods (Lyapunov/alternating optimization, successive convex approximation, deep RL) and distributed methods (multi-agent deep RL, matching theory, auction theory) [152]. Sections V examine how these tools have been adapted to NTN-SemCom.

V Semantic Communication for Satellite Networks

Satellites are the most extensively studied NTN platform for SemCom. The combination of huge data generation (modern Earth-observation satellites can produce terabytes per day), short visibility windows, and limited downlink bandwidth makes the case for SemCom almost self-evident. We divide the literature into six themes: (i) Earth-observation downlink, (ii) channel-adaptive D-JSCC over satellite links, (iii) generative-AI-based satellite SemCom, (iv) multi-hop and inter-satellite SemCom, (v) resource allocation for satellite SemCom, and (vi) federated semantic learning across constellations.

V-A Earth Observation: Semantic Downlink

Earth observation (EO) is the canonical satellite SemCom application. A satellite captures an image (often 10710^{7}-10810^{8} pixels per acquisition) and must downlink the relevant information to a ground station within a brief visibility window. The work of Hassan et al. [95] systematically formulates the problem: a SemCom quality-of-service (SC-QoS) constraint is defined, and the downlink latency is minimized by jointly selecting the JSCC compression ratio and the satellite-gateway association via a discrete whale optimization algorithm and a one-to-one matching game. Compared with traditional JPEG+LDPC, semantic encoding can deliver more meaningful information in a small fraction of the time, freeing the remaining visibility window for additional users or measurements. Building on this, Nguyen et al. [115] pointed out a subtle but important issue: in real LEO constellations, ground users far from the satellite coverage can receive the data via a multi-hop relay through gateways, where hardware equipped with powerful antennas can eliminate accumulated semantic distortion in the latent space. In addition, leveraging the gateway’s unlimited energy, they proposed performing denoising using a small neural network and optimizing gateway-hop selection for low-SNR users. Compared with direct relay, the proposed framework substantially raises the semantic similarity at the receiver, particularly for users at the cell edge. On the other hand, authors in [135] considered the cloud interference in the image and conducted a pre-processing process to derive a cloud-free image before transmitting it through a semantic communication system.

Previous work mainly focuses on the quality of the image; here, we provide a line of work that considers onboard semantic compression. Bhattacharjee and Jung [113] explored semantic compression using a compressed learning framework that relies on fast, sparse matrix-vector multiplication to encode data. In their study, camera noise and the communication channel are the main sources of distortion. Their semantic communication pipeline uses a learned, low-complexity compression matrix to process the noisy camera output and create a vector of observations, which is then sent through the communication channel. Although a deep encoder would yield better compression, a sparse linear encoder fits in the radiation-hardened FPGAs and ASICs that flight satellites can host; finally, the downstream task is performed on the ground. Soret et al. [106] take a system-level view, investigate the integration of SemCom and edge computing for EO applications. They envisioned a distributed edge architecture, where the LEO satellites collaborate to perform the semantic-aware image processing, object detection, and data compression before delivering to ground gateways. They emphasize that energy is a critical constraint: semantic extraction reduces the energy spent on transmission but increases the energy spent on computation, so the optimal split depends on the on-board processor architecture and channel quality.

To support task-oriented EO inference, the visual-event-detection over AI-edge LEO satellites work [105] introduces AoMI as the central metric. The system uses D-JSCC to send only the features needed for event classification, and a threshold-based AoI analysis quantifies the proportion of users that meet timeliness requirements. The result is higher inference accuracy and lower AoMI than those of separate source-channel coding baselines, demonstrating that goal-oriented SemCom is particularly well-suited to time-sensitive EO. The cognitive semantic augmentation framework [154] proposed discrete task-oriented joint source-channel coding (DT-JSCC) with semantic data augmentation, explicitly designing the system around inter-satellite links to enable the analysis and sharing of multispectral imagery across the constellation before any data reaches the ground. This is especially powerful for events that span multiple satellite footprints, such as wildfires or hurricanes. Finally, the work [155] implemented a vector-quantized variational autoencoder to bridge the gap between semantic communication and current digital systems in satellite communication, where a synchronized shared codebook between satellites and ground stations is essential.

V-B Channel-Adaptive SemCom over Satellite Links

Satellite links exhibit large, dynamic SNR variations within a single pass, and the nominal SNR can differ by 10-20 dB between the start and the end of a visibility window. Therefore, researchers have dedicated their effort to develop an adaptive SemCom framework to facilitate this property of Satellites as shown in Fig. 6. The work [156] adopted semantic communication for satellite-integrated Internet over shadowed-Rician (SR) channel, in which they naively adjust communication with Rate Control Policy Network. On the other hand, the work in [157] acknowledged the rapid changes in satellite channel states and proposed a specialized channel predictor to mitigate the impact of outdated CSI, enabling the SemCom to proactively adjust the coding strategy, including the compression rate. The authors in [158] take a step further by incorporating the satellite queue states into the process of adjusting the compression rate, in addition to the time-varying SNR factor. In addition, they offloaded the SNR prediction to the ground gateway, which is contrary to previous works.

Authors of [109] proposed a channel code-book (CCB) that documents the fading and noise states under various channel conditions and dynamically adjusts the denoiser’s parameters at the receiver. The encoder remains fixed, but the decoder is selected from a discrete set of pre-trained options. The granularity of the code-book trades adaptivity against memory. Different from the aforementioned works that mainly consider the image modality, a recent work [100] has developed a multimodal SemCom system to transmit video/speech. Interestingly, they employed an LLM-based agent to dynamically prioritize audio in video streams based on task requirements and channel conditions. Finally, to ensure synchronization of the knowledge base among communicating parties, they implemented a dynamic keyframe update mechanism.

A more aggressive approach is the Doppler-adaptive digital SemCom [137], which integrates a DRL agent with a VQ-VAE to address the fixed modulation that can degrade the system performance in different scenarios. Specifically, the DRL agent observes the predicted Doppler shift and SNR and selects the modulation scheme; the VQ-VAE provides discrete codes compatible with classical digital pipelines. This work is particularly relevant for IoT devices that cannot afford analog SemCom and need to interface with standardized waveforms. The importance-aware robust semantic transmission (IRST) framework of Cao et al. [94] prioritizes the semantically vital content based on real-time channel state. They first segment the image into different regions and then determine their relevance to the current task. Finally, a SNR-aware channel codec for adaptive channel coding and a semantic selection mechanism to drop low-importance regions when bandwidth is tight. On a remote-sensing dataset, IRST consistently outperforms a fixed-rate D-JSCC baseline, especially at low SNR.

V-C Generative-AI-Based Satellite SemCom

The arrival of large generative models has profoundly influenced satellite SemCom. The motivation is simple: under harsh channel conditions, classical reconstructions look “glitchy” (block artifacts, unnatural colors), whereas a generative decoder can hallucinate content that, while not identical to the source, is photo-realistic and task-equivalent [159]. An early work [160] has adopted this SemCom direction for general communication, building a generative AI-empowered semantic knowledge base that converts an input image into a “prompt”, which consumes significantly less bandwidth. The work [18] is not limited to SemCom in satellite systems; it also explores the potential of Generative AI for space resource allocation and network deployment, particularly its capacity to enhance the security and privacy of diffusion models by detecting anomalies in data flows.

Jiang et al. [93] proposed FMSAT, a foundation-model-based semantic satellite communication framework, where they utilized SegGPT for semantic segmentation at the transmitter. At the receiver, a conditional diffusion model is used to generate the target image conditioned on the corrupted input signal. Besides this, to avoid long propagation delays, the authors designed a novel error detection method: a rough detector at the satellite to quickly check without reconstructing the data, and a fine detector at the gateway to guarantee the quality of the received image. The work in [161] introduced a generative-AI-assisted framework for satellite communications, where LLMs and retrieval-augmented generation were leveraged to support the formulation of complex mathematical models using satellite-domain expert knowledge. Building upon this AI-driven modeling paradigm, the authors further proposed a mixture-of-experts-based proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework, in which multiple specialized experts collaboratively optimize different transmission variables and aggregate their decisions through a gating network to improve communication performance under satellite interference and large-scale network complexity. Recognizing the potential of Generative-semCom, [162] designed a dynamic resource allocation algorithm to maximize the multi-objective functions, including power consumption, bandwidth efficiency, and data fidelity, thereby enhancing the potential GSC in diverse satellite applications

V-D Multi-Hop and Inter-Satellite Semantic Transmission

An LEO mega-constellation is, in essence, an in-orbit packet-switched network connected by ISLs. Routing semantic content across this network raises new questions that go beyond the conventional shortest-path or minimum-hop-count formulations [163]: in particular, the right routing decision for semantic content is the one that maximizes end-to-end semantic fidelity, not the one that maximizes per-hop bit rate. This insight motivates the emerging research direction of joint semantic coding and routing. For instance, [81] modeled the dynamic multi-hop LEO satellite network as a time-varying directed graph:

𝒢⁡(t)=(𝒱,ℰ⁡(t)),\mathcal{G}(t)=\left(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{E}(t)\right), (7)

where 𝒱\mathcal{V} and ℰ⁡(t)\mathcal{E}(t) denote the satellite set and time-varying inter-satellite links (ISLs), respectively. The forwarding decision at each satellite ii is formulated as a factorized joint action:

𝐚i​(t)=(aihop​(t),aic​(t),airelay​(t)),\mathbf{a}_{i}(t)=\left(a_{i}^{\mathrm{hop}}(t),\ a_{i}^{c}(t),\ a_{i}^{\mathrm{relay}}(t)\right), (8)

where aihop​(t)a_{i}^{\mathrm{hop}}(t) selects the next hop, aic​(t)a_{i}^{c}(t) allocates the semantic channel budget, and airelay​(t)a_{i}^{\mathrm{relay}}(t) determines whether relay-side semantic re-encoding is activated. Based on this formulation, the authors proposed GraphJSCR, a graph attention network (GAT)-enhanced reinforcement learning framework that leverages local topology and transmission states for adaptive hop-by-hop semantic routing under dynamic network conditions. In their evaluation, GraphJSCR consistently maintains the lowest end-to-end latency under heavy semantic-session loads. Complementarily, Guo et al. [164] identified a structural constraint unique to SC routing in mega-constellations: every feasible path must traverse at least one AI-equipped satellite whose semantic encoder shares the same KB as the destination ground station, rendering classical contact graph routing (CGR) inapplicable. Modeling user, relay, and AI satellites jointly within a temporal graph, they formulate SC-aware routing as an integer linear program with explicit KB-matching and post-encoding capacity constraints, and propose a polynomial-time algorithm based on forward- and backward-shortest-path precomputation followed by SC-aware path joining at AI satellites. Starlink-scale simulations show substantial gains in acceptance ratio, throughput, and end-to-end delay over CGR.

To mitigate semantic noise accumulation in satellite relay networks, [117] proposes a Semantic Forwarding-based Semantic Communication (SFSC) framework for LEO satellite-terrestrial networks. Unlike conventional regenerative relaying, which performs full decoding and re-encoding at the satellite, the proposed framework introduces a lightweight semantic forwarder that operates directly at the codebook-index level, avoiding redundant semantic distortion while significantly reducing on-board computational overhead. A FiLM-based channel-aware reconstruction scheme further enhances robustness under dynamic LEO channel conditions. From a complementary perspective, Huang et al. [165] extend multi-satellite semantic transmission to direct satellite-to-user access under stringent link budgets, treating ISLs as a task-migration plane rather than a pure forwarding fabric. Their framework couples three transmission modes (bit, text-only semantic, and hybrid token-plus-text) with a controllable number of diffusion denoising steps at the receiver, and introduces an adaptive-weighted semantic efficiency metric that jointly trades off latency, generation quality, and on-device computation. Mode selection, satellite-user association, ISL migration, denoising depth, and metric weights are jointly optimized via a decision-assisted REINFORCE++ scheme with feasibility-aware action masking, showing clear gains over fixed-weight baselines. There is still limited work on multi-hop semantic communication for satellite networks, while a couple of works on multi-hop SemCom and relay/forwarding have been proposed. The authors in [166] considered the accumulation error problem in multi-hop semantic communication and addressed it by proposing a recursive training method in a general framework.

V-E Resource Allocation for Satellite SemCom

Resource allocation in NTN-SemCom is fundamentally different from that in classical satellite communication. The reason is twofold. First, in SemCom, the relationship between allocated bandwidth/power and the receiver’s task accuracy is not a closed-form function; it depends on the encoder/decoder, the channel, and the task [20]. Second, SemCom introduces a new optimization variable-the semantic compression ratio-that simultaneously affects extraction latency, transmission latency, and receiver-side processing latency, often in opposing directions. Therefore, the resource allocation problem for the SemCom Satellite is highly scenario-dependent, making direct comparison difficult. For instance, the work [167] proposed a minimization of energy objective consumed by the satellite and UAVs, while ensuring transmission is completed within the window time and coverage areas. They control the locations of UAVs, the compression rate of SemCom, and, finally, the ratio between computing and communication resources. On the other hand, the authors in [168] proposed a specialized metric called Quality of Semantic, in which they optimized transmit power, bandwidth, the number of semantic symbols, and, finally, computation resources to maximize this value. In this work, they adopted soft-actor critics DRL as the solution, while the previous work leveraged the block-coordinate descent technique. In the meantime, the work [172] focused on minimizing the latency from satellite to users with three variables: predefined accuracy, power consumption, and finally, CPU frequency of users. Instead of modeling the relation between SNR, compression rate, and the quality of SemCom [170] conducted an empirical experiment to obtain grid results and approximate the relation with a curve-fitting model, which converts the remaining resource allocation as in traditional communication.

V-F Federated SemCom Learning across Satellites

Training a SemCom encoder/decoder traditionally requires a centralized dataset. In LEO constellations, however, each satellite continually generates fresh imagery that, for privacy or sovereignty reasons, may not be gathered at a single training cloud, which can be resolved by federated learning. The SemSpaceFL framework [104] considered each satellite train a local semantic encoder-decoder on its own imagery, then transmitted the model updates with regional gateways during their visibility windows. The distributed gateways collected all the updated models and to perform intermediate aggregation, weighting each satellite’s contribution by the number of data samples, training epochs, and loss. A two-tier (satellite-to-gateway, gateway-to-cloud) aggregation scheme reduces communication overhead and respects the constellation’s heterogeneity. Empirically, SemSpaceFL achieves higher reconstruction quality than other conventional FL while completing training within a few orbits.

A parallel thread, the proposal in [118], addresses the case where different satellites are running different tasks, such as segmentation, classification, or detection, in which naively averaging models trained on different tasks can be destructive. Motivated to address the issue, the authors proposed a semantic-aware task clustering mechanism, which groups tasks based on their semantic similarity. A similarity threshold determines whether two tasks should belong to the same cluster, while a transitivity constraint guarantees non-overlapping. An interesting scenario was proposed in [171], where they adopted semantic communication to offload the task from satellites to ground stations, in the same time considering the pruning-split federated learning for the SemCom. In the meantime, the problem of cross-domain is worth studying [173], where the data from the client can originate from different sources. In the NTN scenario, sensing images captured from diverse orbits may cover different regions (desert, forest, sea, and city), which can negatively affect the general learning objective.

V-G Summary and Lessons Learned

This section has provided novel research works of SemCom under the satellite networks, spanning from earth observation to segmentation applications, and how it can address the dynamic changes in channel state of the satellite, along with the communication scenario when the bandwidth is scarce. The summary and takeaway lessons are listed below:

  • •

    The dominant paradigm SemCom framework is D-JSCC, where the joint optimization between source and channel coder provides certain robustness under extreme channel conditions of the satellite network. Unlike conventional systems, the DL-enabled SemCom can predict SNR values and proactively adjust its coding strategy, such as the compression rate or the prioritization of essential regions, to adapt to time-varying SNR.

  • •

    Generative AI-enabled SemCom has emerged as a promising solution when the available communication resources at the satellites are extremely low or harsh channels. In this scenario, the transmitter can convert the target image into text, prompts, or segment-level descriptions, consuming only a fraction of the bandwidth required by the original data. However, the main cost is the large amount of computing resources at the receiver, where it’s required to generate data that possesses semantic similarity to the original, which is acceptable at ground gateways but problematic for the satellite.

  • •

    To substantially extend satellite coverage, multi-hop SemCom, including semantic-forward relaying and semantic-aware routing, has been studied and redesigned from the ground up to account for the semantic objective function, energy constraints, and satellite network dynamics. Specifically, semantic relay nodes must preserve end-to-end fidelity while minimizing energy and latency.

  • •

    With the vast volume of observational data continuously captured from LEO orbits, FL offers a principled and privacy-preserving approach for training SemCom models across LEO constellations without centralizing sensitive satellite imagery. However, due to the inherent dynamics of satellite movement, a carefully designed aggregation architecture and clustering strategy are required to ensure an effective and coherent federation framework.

VI SemCom for UAV and HAPS Networks

Unlike satellites, UAVs fly at lower altitudes, can be deployed quickly, and can change their paths easily, but they are limited in size, weight, and power. These features have led to a large amount of SemCom research, which we divide into four main areas. The first area focuses on compressing bandwidth and energy use for UAV images and video, often using deep joint source-channel coding (D-JSCC). The second area is cognitive UAV SemCom, where sharing knowledge graphs with ground stations improves object detection and helps reduce semantic noise. The third area looks at optimizing both UAV flight paths and SemCom resources, usually with reinforcement learning. The fourth area uses federated learning to train semantic models, even when connections are unstable and onboard resources are limited. Finally, we discuss SemCom for HAPS, whose design is between UAVs and satellites in terms of altitude, endurance, and cost.

VI-A D-JSCC for UAV Image and Video Transmission

The work in [174] proposed D-JSCC for wildfire detection in UAVs, where they exploit the flexibility and easy-to-deploy property of UAVs. Specifically, they equipped the camera on the UAV to capture the image of interest regions, which were later encoded by the D-JSCC encoder. As the task demands a fast response, it directly skips the reconstruction and conducts the prediction based on the received encoded feature. Finally, the work identified an insight that the UAV’s height has a complex impact on the detection accuracy. Another application of SemCom-assisted UAVs was proposed in [175], where a UAV captures images of an apple orchard to identify ripe apples. Specifically, the work leverages the YOLO framework to detect apples in the captured images, after which the UAV transmits only the image regions containing apples. The masked image consumes only a small amount of communication bandwidth and energy compared with the unmasked one.

On the other hand, the work [176] used DRL to identify the most meaningful blocks in captured images for the task at back-end edge computing. The author introduced the reward function for both the scene classification accuracy and transmission latency, which obtains a good balance for the aerial transmission paradigm. [177] approached the limitations of computing and communication resources of UAV from a different angle; they decomposed the image into coarse and fine-grained semantic information, where they obtained coarse-grained information by retrieving a codeword that best matches the target image from a pre-constructed codebook. The fine-grained component is constructed by a lightweight encoder and transmitted through a data channel to the receiver, while coarse-grained is delivered through a telemetry channel before being fused together at the receiver.

Robust transmission for low-altitude UAVs is the focus of the work [178], where the authors observe that a UAV image can be decomposed into a structure component and a stochastic texture component. Therefore, they proposed a Structure-Texture VAE to explicitly disentangle the image, enabling different error protection strategies, in which the framework prioritizes geometric skeletons. Finally, under the restricted budgets, the receiver employs a conditional generative model to handle the missing textures and obtains a 5.65.6 dB gain in PSNR compared to standard D-JSCC. The authors in [179] noted that previous work mainly focused on analog transmission, which is susceptible to channel noise and difficult to integrate with current digital hardware. Therefore, they proposed a context-adaptive digital semantic communication design, where the address not only encodes an analog signal but also provides a context prompt to assist the SemCom in executing the task. The system delivers up to a 22% gain in semantic-structural similarity and a 14% reduction in age of information compared with prior UAV-SemCom baselines.

VI-B Knowledge-Graph-Driven Cognitive UAV SemCom

Cognitive semantic communication (CSC) offers a new approach for UAVs by using a knowledge graph to boost transmission efficiency and task accuracy. In  [102], the UAV applies a multi-scale parallel codec, which uses five single-scale residual compressors aligned with feature-pyramid levels. This setup compresses semantic features at different levels while keeping important details for small aerial objects. Instead of reconstructing lossy images like traditional methods, the receiver combines its own knowledge-graph information with visual proposals to form a weighted graph. This graph is then improved by a relational graph attention network (R-GAT), which helps make better use of object relationships and corrects errors from noise and compression. On a real aerial-image dataset, this system achieves higher detection accuracy using much less bandwidth, with only a 0.6% drop in accuracy under Rayleigh fading, compared to a 7.4% drop for the JPEG+LDPC baseline.

The study in  [180] brought personalized saliency into task-oriented SemCom, addressing the gap where earlier research overlooked user differences. Their method combines objective visual attention from RelTR triplet detection with each user’s own saliency heatmaps, using a tunable fusion coefficient to decide which triplets to send to each user. Turning these personalized saliency maps into triplets also helps reduce the UAV’s memory use. The paper also calculates the probability of semantic triplet loss under the realistic Fisher-Snedecor FF fading channel, instead of treating the channel as a black box. Recognizing the value of knowledge graphs,  [181] explored using a knowledge graph with adversarial training to fight semantic noise. To build the knowledge graph, they divided the image into patches, processed them with a Vision Transformer’s self-attention layers, used a GPT-2 text decoder to create a natural-language description, and then extracted triplets to form the graph.

VI-C Trajectory and Resource Optimization for UAV SemCom

Recognizing that prior UAV studies emphasized SemCom design while overlooking resource optimization, the authors of [149] formulated a resource allocation problem that jointly maximizes a proposed quality-of-service metric and minimizes communication resource consumption, controlling the number of transmitted semantic symbols, transmit power, and bandwidth. Bringing the flight path into the same optimization, the work [182] employed four cooperating soft actor-critic agents that jointly optimize the UAV trajectory, the number of semantic symbols, and the transmit power for a single-UAV data-gathering system. The work [183] instead maximized the total similarity metric across all users by jointly optimizing the UAV trajectory, semantic information selection, and UAV-user association. In a similar multi-user setting but targeting spectral efficiency, the NOMA-based framework of [184] superposes the semantic streams of co-channel users on a shared band and jointly optimizes the number of semantic symbols, the UAV trajectories, and the power allocation to maximize the semantic sum rate, periodically grouping users with an improved K-means clustering scheme and solving the allocation with a shared dueling double deep Q-network. Treating the UAV as a mobile base station that must serve users whose locations and task demands are unknown a priori, the authors of [185] let the UAV jointly adjust its flight path and transmitter encoder compression ratio and then return to the supply point within the maximum flight time.

Addressing UAV-based image collection from IoT devices, the authors of [186] integrated semantic communication with UAV command and control, in which each IoT device encodes its image via D-JSCC into an importance-ordered latent vector that supports reconstruction from a partially received symbol set. A base station steers the UAV through acceleration commands to maximize the average reconstructed-image quality over a fixed time horizon. Unlike the trajectory-optimization works above, the command-and-control downlink is not assumed delay-free; the problem is modeled as an MDP and solved by a Double Deep Q-Network flight policy. Two further studies make the mission-level objective explicit: the work [187] minimizes the time for a semantic data-collection mission over a remote area while balancing reconstruction quality against the energy cost of computation, employing a reinforcement learning agent with a hybrid discrete-continuous action space to jointly handle the trajectory and the extraction decisions, whereas [188] targets information freshness, adaptively selecting whether semantic extraction is performed at the UAVs or at the ground users based on real-time data size and channel conditions and minimizing the semantic-aware age of information through a Lyapunov-guided DRL policy whose deployment subproblem is refined by alternating optimization and successive convex approximation.

The aforementioned problems are all solved within a DRL framework, albeit with different policies. In contrast, the authors of [189] addressed post-disaster emergency communication, where multiple UAVs use semantic communication to transmit extracted “ideas” instead of raw data. To minimize the total UAV energy consumption-dominated by flight and hovering-while meeting user demands, they distribute the workload across UAVs, assigning each either a request-collection-and-encoding or a data-forwarding role, and solve the resulting scheduling problem with Monte Carlo Tree Search rather than a learning-based policy. Also targeting post-disaster relief, the authors of [190] investigated a multi-UAV data collection and semantic forwarding network, in which clustered UAVs perform intra-cluster semantic aggregation and then act as virtual antenna arrays relaying the extracted information to a remote base station via collaborative beamforming. They formulated a multi-objective problem jointly maximizing the user and semantic transmission rates while minimizing UAV flight energy, controlling the clustering, UAV locations, excitation current weights, and semantic symbols per word. Since the resulting mixed-integer nonlinear program has a clustering-dependent decision dimensionality, an alternating-optimization approach was proposed in which a large language model tunes the evolutionary-search parameters, rather than the problem being solved by a learning-based policy.

A parallel line of work eschews learning-based policies in favor of classical optimization machinery with explicit guarantees. Liang et al. [191] consider a multi-antenna UAV serving fluid-antenna-equipped users, jointly optimizing the UAV trajectory, transmit beamforming, semantic compression rate, and the selection of activated fluid-antenna ports to maximize the minimum equivalent rate among all users via an alternating algorithm. From an energy-focused perspective, the agentic-AI design in [192] jointly optimizes semantic compression, UAV deployment, and AI-inference-task offloading, recognizing that deeper compression reduces transmission energy but raises on-board computation energy; its agentic-AI controller manages these decisions jointly and outperforms a block-coordinate-descent baseline prone to local optima.

Exploiting the UAV’s dual role as both a server and a sensing node, [193] proposed a joint edge computing and semantic communication scheme for UAV-enabled networks, in which the UAV extracts scene graphs from captured images and transmits them to a ground base station while simultaneously acting as an edge server that executes computing tasks offloaded from ground users. Extending the UAV-assisted MEC setting to an adversarial environment, the authors of [194] investigated multi-UAV-assisted MEC in the Internet of Vehicles, where multiple UAVs collect image semantic tasks from vehicles and text semantic tasks from roadside units while a jammer disrupts the channels. Their objective is to minimize the total communication and computation delay and maximize the semantic accuracy by jointly optimizing the UAV trajectories, user associations, and channel selection. To handle the non-convex problem in such a dynamic and adversarial environment, a multi-agent DRL algorithm, namely SC-MA-TD3, was proposed to foster cooperation among the UAVs.

VI-D UAV-assisted Federated Learning SemCom

Targeting semantic communication within a UAV swarm, where the dynamic topology and volatile links hinder the training of accurate semantic models on resource-limited UAVs, the authors of [195] proposed a hierarchical federated learning architecture that organizes the swarm into clusters led by cluster heads. Specifically, intra-cluster training adopts centralized federated learning in which UAVs upload model parameters to their cluster head, whereas inter-cluster training adopts decentralized federated learning among neighboring cluster heads, thereby combining the low communication overhead of the former with the robustness of the latter. To incentivize the participation of self-interested UAVs, the cluster selection was further formulated as an evolutionary game, and a cluster management mechanism was designed to handle UAV dropout caused by link faults.

To address the size, weight, and power (SWAP) constraints that limit a UAV’s capacity to run deep-learning-based semantic extraction on-board, the authors of [196] introduced federated learning as a distributed training framework for UAV semantic communication. Specifically, the edge users collaboratively train the joint source-channel coding semantic model while the UAV serves only as the central aggregator, thereby relieving the resource-constrained UAV of the computational burden of model training. Using this framework, we set up a joint optimization problem to reduce the energy-delay product and ensure fair quality of service for all users. The control variables were the UAV flight path and bandwidth allocation. We modeled the problem as an MDP and solved it with a single-agent PPO algorithm [197].

VI-E Semantic Communication in HAPS Networks

Research on SemCom for HAPS is still limited, mainly because of cost and deployment challenges: UAVs are cheap and easy to use, which makes them good for experiments. Satellites cost more at first, but their value increases over time. HAPS fall in between: they are more expensive and harder to operate than UAVs, but they do not offer the same coverage or long-term benefits as satellites. The study [198] looks at a SemCom-based NTN downlink, where an LEO satellite extracts semantic features from Earth images and sends them to several HAPS, which act as semantic receivers. The authors introduce QoSem, a metric that measures semantic rate, accuracy, and processing time together. They also set up a joint optimization problem for transmit power, bandwidth, computation, and semantic-symbol selection, which they solve using a mixed-action DRL algorithm. In the work, HAPS are used only as basic relay receivers, not as unique stratospheric platforms.

Nkurunziza and Umehara [199] address the problem of semantic eavesdropping, where an unauthorized receiver can pick up important features over the open HAPS-to-ground channel. They combine channel and spatial attention for node optimization and use a two-part protection method. First, Gaussian differential privacy hides the extracted image features. Second, a learned feature-transformation layer scrambles these features so that only the intended receiver can recover them using an inverse transformation. This approach keeps the reconstruction quality high for the legitimate receiver, while the eavesdropper’s quality stays very low.

VI-F Summary and Lessons Learned

This section reviews SemCom research in UAV and HAPS networks, covering four main UAV topics: D-JSCC-based compression, knowledge-graph-driven cognitive SemCom, joint trajectory and resource optimization, and UAV-assisted federated learning. We also include the emerging HAPS-focused studies. Table V lists these approaches and their references. From this review, we highlight several key lessons:

  • •

    UAV SemCom is mainly shaped by strict size, weight, and power limits. These constraints drive design choices like lightweight encoders, masked or region-of-interest transmission, and codebook-based representations, all aimed at fitting semantic extraction into a UAV’s limited computing and energy resources. Practical UAV SemCom systems should be judged not just on accuracy, but also on their onboard computational demands.

  • •

    Since a UAV’s position can be controlled, the best outcomes come from optimizing trajectory, resource allocation, and semantic-symbol selection together. This approach leads to complex problems, often solved with DRL and rarely with formal guarantees. While these methods work well in simulations, their performance in real-world channels and missions is still mostly untested.

  • •

    Cognitive, knowledge-graph-driven methods improve robustness by correcting errors from noise and compression through inter-object relationships. However, they require maintaining and synchronizing a knowledge base between the UAV and the ground. FL shifts model training away from the resource-limited UAV, but it still faces challenges like changing network structures, link failures, and node dropout. Solutions such as hierarchical clustering, evolutionary game-based participation, or using the UAV as an aggregator show promise.

  • •

    SemCom for HAPS is much less studied compared to UAVs and satellites.
