Most current research treats HAPS as a basic relay receiver or sender and does not use its unique stratospheric features, such as quasi-stationary positioning, long endurance, and stable wide-area line-of-sight links. Addressing this gap is an important direction for future research and motivates the resource-allocation and security challenges discussed in the next section.

VII Semantic Communication for Integrated SAGIN/SAGSIN

When LEO, MEO, and GEO satellites, HAPS, UAVs, ground users, and maritime nodes are combined, the resulting integrated network is fundamentally different from any single part. In this context, SemCom faces challenges like multi-hop propagation, varying link quality, strict and uneven resource limits, and fast-changing network structures. Resource allocation issues also become interconnected across different layers. As a result, research has moved in several directions: broad architectural approaches that rethink semantics for the entire network; multi-tier relay frameworks designed for satellite, UAV, and ground integration; resource-efficient methods that link semantic compression with computing and energy use; solutions for mobility and changing network structures; and generative AI as a key enabler. This section reviews each of these areas.

VII-A Architectural Visions

Uysal [108] studied goal-oriented semantic communication in a diverse NTN setup that includes LEO and GEO satellites, HAPS, and ground IoT devices. The approach focuses on sending only the most relevant data at each stage. Ground sensors use AoI-based sampling before accessing the channel, HAPS and satellites handle scheduling and queue management based on goals, and the bundle protocol in delay-tolerant networking manages semantic flow control at each hop. Together, these steps help keep information relevant from end to end, even when delays vary. Qiu et al. [200] look at situational awareness and operations management in the space-air-ground-sea integrated network (SAGSIN). They argue that traditional digital twins, which rely on lots of data, stable links, and strong computing resources, do not fit SAGSIN’s large, fast-changing, and resource-limited environment. Instead, they introduce the goal-oriented semantic twin (GOST), a new approach that values task usefulness over exact physical detail. GOST has three layers: knowledge-based semantics, data-driven semantics, and goal-oriented principles. The paper also reviews supporting technologies, a multi-dimensional evaluation method, and a case study on tracking multiple UAVs remotely. This work shifts the focus of twinning in SAGSIN to semantic, lightweight, and task-specific models. Gao et al. [201] see SAGIN nodes changing from passive communication relays to intelligent agents powered by large language models. They propose the multi-agent intelligent networking (MAIN) architecture. MAIN uses semantic intelligence to combine task-driven semantic signaling, semantic routing, and an intent-driven management system across domains. This approach shifts SAGIN networking to focus on completing missions efficiently instead of just transmitting content.

VII-B Multi-Tier Relay Frameworks

One key feature of SAGIN is its multi-tier relay structure. Data moves from a satellite to a UAV or HAPS, and then to ground users, with each step having its own channel quality. Semantic communication needs to be designed to work across these linked stages.

Waqas et al. [202] introduced a Perception-Aware Hybrid-Action DRL (PAHA-DRL) framework for joint task offloading and collaborative uplink beamforming in three-tier SAGIN. UAVs with mmWave radar and vision sensors gather real-time data on user density, blockage, and link quality, which is then used by a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) agent working in a hybrid action space. Block coordinate descent and successive convex approximation (SCA) help define the possible actions, while constraint-aware masking ensures delay, power, and SNR requirements are met. Their results show a 92% offloading success rate and a 38.9% reduction in delay compared to greedy baselines, supporting the value of perception-driven resource coordination across tiers.

To expand semantic services beyond single-cluster setups, Yin et al. [203] studied a downlink SAGIN where a satellite serves several ground clusters through UAV relays. Their main innovation is a dual-mode relay: each UAV can either send semantic symbols directly to users with computation ability or convert them into bit streams for conventional users. This approach keeps semantic communication efficient while reaching devices with fewer resources. The authors optimize transmit power, bandwidth, and UAV positions to maximize the sum-rate, solving the problem by alternating optimization (AO) between convex subproblems. This work advances the design of relays for multi-cluster, mixed-user networks, which earlier point-to-point studies did not address.

Huang et al. [112] developed a hybrid bit-and-generative semantic communication framework for downlink image transmission in a three-tier SAGIN. In this setup, LEO satellites with scalable semantic encoders send data to ground users through UAV relays. The framework supports three transmission modes: traditional bit-based (JPEG2000), text-only generation, and text-plus-image embedding using latent diffusion. This allows for flexible tradeoffs between quality and latency, even with strict satellite link budgets. The authors introduce a new Semantic Communication Efficiency (SCE) metric that measures both reconstruction quality and delay. They also use a Distributional Soft Actor-Critic (DSAC) algorithm to jointly optimize UAV paths, UAV-satellite pairing, inter-satellite link choices, and transmission mode, helping the system adapt to changing SAGIN conditions.

VII-C Resource-Efficient SemCom: Compression, Computation, and Energy

Another area of research focuses on the significant and uneven resource limitations of non-terrestrial platforms. This work looks at how to balance semantic compression with the costs of computation and energy. Liu et al. [204] introduced a resource allocation framework for MEC-assisted SAGIN that brings together LEO satellites, UAV relays, and ground IoT devices. Their Probabilistic Semantic Compression (PSC) method reduces the amount of data sent before tasks are offloaded along the UE to UAV to LEO path. They use joint optimization to cut down on both task delay and energy use. The problem is split into UAV deployment using SCA and a subproblem for offloading, compression, and resource allocation, which is solved with Multi-Agent PPO (MAPPO). Their results show up to 78.4% less energy use compared to local processing, showing that PSC helps balance compression, computation, and energy across different SAGIN layers.

Zhao et al. [114] were the first to focus on resource allocation for semantic communication in SAGIN. They studied a downlink from satellite to UAV to ground terminal, where both the satellite and UAV use shared probabilistic graphs as a common knowledge base for PSCom. The balance between compression and computation is described using a piecewise overhead function Ok​(ρk)O_{k}(\rho_{k}): lower compression ratios require more complex conditional probabilities, which increases computation cost. Their joint optimization problem covers UAV location, beamwidth, bandwidth, power, compression ratios, and how tasks are split between satellite and UAV. They break this into six subproblems, finding closed-form solutions for computation capacity and UAV altitude at each step. Their approach uses less energy than non-semantic or simpler methods.

VII-D Semantic Transmission under Mobility and Dynamic Topology

The high speeds of LEO satellites and the rapid changes in SAGIN topologies cause Doppler distortion, frequent handovers, and limited observability. The studies discussed here focus on solving these challenges. Liu et al. [205] introduce OTFSSC, an end-to-end semantic communication system that combines Deep JSCC with OTFS modulation to handle high-speed mobility, such as LEO satellite links (NTN-TDL-A) and V2X channels. The system extracts semantic features, encodes them with JSCC, and maps them onto delay-Doppler grids using a chunk mapping method to reduce ICI and ISI. At the receiver, an Enhanced Reconstruction Diffusion Model (ERDM) uses its generative abilities to correct for Doppler distortion and channel noise. The Semi-OTFS-MA scheme builds on this by allowing high- and low-mobility users to transmit at the same time without SIC. Theoretical analyses of rate and power regions support the semantic transmission rate framework.[206] address vertical handover decision-making in ISAC-enabled SAGIN by proposing a Diffusion Model-based GAI-empowered Handover Decision (DGHD) algorithm. Operating across LEO satellite and ground network tiers, the framework models handover as a multiobjective optimization minimizing jitter and load difference while maximizing robustness. DGHD replaces the conventional policy network in MAPPO, leveraging DDPM’s reverse denoising process to generate optimal handover decisions under high-dimensional, time-varying SAGIN dynamics. Validated against Starlink/OneWeb constellations with real mobility datasets, DMAPPO outperforms MADDPG, MAPPO, and QMIX, demonstrating strong scalability across constellation sizes from 1,000 to 2,500 satellites. Jia et al. [207] present a semantic graph-based MARL framework for service migration and request routing in satellite-supported low-altitude UAV networks. In these networks, the fast-changing topology and limited local information make centralized control impractical. The framework uses a discrete denoising diffusion model (DiGress) to create varied, realistic satellite-UAV network topologies that reflect changing loads. A cyclic recurrent message-passing method spreads local semantic features, such as structural centrality, satellite node details, and packet statistics, across the graph to estimate the global state. Agents then use DQN [208] and these enriched graph observations to make distributed routing and migration decisions, leading to lower transmission delays and better throughput compared to non-semantic and non-recurrent methods.

VII-E Generative AI as a Cross-Cutting Enabler

While the preceding works apply generative models to specific tasks, generative AI also functions as a broad enabler spanning the entire integrated network. The generative-AI-for-SAGIN tutorial of Zhang et al. [18] provides a panoramic view of how generative models can be deployed throughout the network: for channel modeling and CSI estimation, joint resource allocation, intelligent network deployment, semantic communications, image extraction and processing, and security. As a case study, they propose a Generative Diffusion Model (GDM) framework that constructs a channel information map for SAGIN, demonstrating substantial QoS improvements.

VII-F Summary and Lessons Learned

This section has reviewed SemCom research on fully integrated SAGIN/SAGSIN systems, where space, air, ground, and maritime layers work together as one network. These systems face unique challenges, such as multi-hop connections, uneven link quality, limited and unevenly spread resources, and rapidly changing network structures. The studies discussed cover topics like network architecture, multi-layer relay systems, joint compression and computation, reliable transmission for moving nodes, and the use of generative AI across these areas. The main lessons learned, each suggesting a possible direction for future research, are listed below:

  • •

    Under this paradigm, SemCom is moving from the link layer to the entire network architecture. Therefore, the objective is not only to be a better codec, but also to be a guiding principle for the whole network. Approaches such as goal-oriented twins, intent-driven networking, and semantic routing have emerged to address this vision.

  • •

    In SAGIN SemCom, the multi-tier relay is the main building block, with each hop serving a different function. The satellite-UAV-ground communication chain exhibits significant variations across hops in terms of channel conditions, computational capability, and service requirements. These heterogeneous characteristics motivate the development of highly adaptive frameworks capable of dynamically managing relay operations, network topology, and robustness against link degradation/failures.

  • •

    Numerous works reveal tight connections among compression rate, computing resources, and energy in SemCom-assisted SAGIN: lowering the compression ratio cuts transmitted data but raises encoding and decoding cost, so these quantities cannot be optimized in isolation. The need to jointly optimize them to meet delay and energy targets becomes far harder across heterogeneous satellites, UAVs, and IoT devices with uneven budgets. Consequently, solutions must operate effectively in distributed, collaborative environments rather than relying on centralized control.

  • •

    LEO satellites are bound to face strong Doppler shifts and connectivity, which is inevitable. To accommodate this property, it is essential to design a mechanism to model and approximately compensate for the Doppler shift effect. In addition, UAV and HAP layers can be deployed as relaying traffic nodes that move slowly relative to the user and can neglect the Doppler shift.

VIII Open Challenges and Future Directions

Regardless of the advancement of SemCom in NTNs, there are several issues that remain unsolved across all platforms. This section is dedicated to providing a complete picture of those challenges, potential solutions, and most promising techniques for advancing SemCom in future NTNs.

VIII-A Resource Allocation and Goal-Oriented Optimization

Resource allocation in classical wireless systems through power, bandwidth, time, and frequency control involves well-developed convex or concave optimization machinery due to the relationship between the allocated resources and the achieved data rate is captured by the Shannon formula. On the other hand, SemCom has broken this clean relationship, creating a complex scenario in which receiver-side task accuracy is an implicit and generally non-differentiable function of the encoder/decoder weights, the channel, and the dataset. In addition, the dynamic compression rate of SemCom to combat the time-varying channel of NTN further complicates the problem. The literature has converged on three broad strategies to obtain a resource-to-accuracy map as follows:

  • •

    Curve fitting: fit a smooth surrogate Q^​(ρ,SNR)\hat{Q}(\rho,\text{SNR}) to the (compression ratio ρ\rho, SNR)-to-quality mapping using a held-out validation set, and then plug Q^\hat{Q} into a classical optimization. The approach is computationally light and can reuse the entire classical toolbox.

  • •

    Reinforcement learning: treat the resource-allocation problem as a Markov decision process and learn a policy that maximizes the long-run task accuracy. PPO, TQC, DQN, dueling-DQN have been adopted in the literature.

  • •

    Joint training of the encoder and the resource-allocation policy: the encoder is trained with a curriculum that simulates the resource constraints, and then the resource-allocator operates on the same learned latent space. In simple words, SemCom and allocation policy are co-adapted rather than optimized in sequence.

None of the three strategies is yet a settled answer; each trades fidelity, sample cost, and adaptability differently, and the field has not converged on when to prefer one. As shown in Table VII, we present additional open challenges, their current states, core difficulties.

VIII-B Freshness and Energy-Aware Semantic Scheduling

In status-update applications like sensor telemetry, remote infrastructure health checks, and Earth observation, the key factor is how up-to-date the data is, not how much is sent. For example, a flood map is only useful while the floodwaters are still present. Therefore, metrics such as TOSSE [94], AoMI [105], and version-AoI [110, 111] are designed to measure how fresh information is. When using these metrics, scheduling tends to prioritize a few recent updates instead of many outdated ones. SemCom builds on this by focusing on semantic freshness. It sends an update only when there is a meaningful change in the underlying state, rather than just tracking raw data freshness.

Delfani and Pappas [110] demonstrated this approach using an energy-harvesting IoT device that collects data and sends it to a network of interconnected LEO satellites. By selecting an update policy that reduces version-AoI across the network, they found that semantics-aware scheduling avoids sending outdated or irrelevant data, which can improve energy efficiency by up to 73%. The semantics-aware unified terrestrial-non-terrestrial 6G framework [111] extends this concept to integrated TN-NTN environments, clearly showing the balance between freshness, relevance, and utility. The significance of these studies is not in the complexity of their encoders, as they often focus on deciding if data should be sent rather than what data to send. Their main contribution is highlighting the shift in SemCom from traditional bit-rate metrics to goal-oriented measures.

In NTN, freshness and energy are closely linked: a scheduler skips stale updates to keep information relevant and save energy, so these goals should be considered together. Regardless, most SemCom papers focus on PSNR or MS-SSIM and do not account for the energy required to compute them, even though energy per task is the primary constraint in NTN. The probabilistic-SemCom-SAGIN work of [114] and the EH-LEO work of [110] are early examples that include computation energy. Further research is expected to examine semantic schedulers that adjust computation based on energy harvesting, especially during eclipse periods, with a greater focus on cross-layer scheduling that accounts for energy needs in attitude control, thermal management, and computation, as well as tracking the energy used to train SemCom models. For decoders based on foundation models, training can use much more energy than day-to-day operations. Training a billion parameters of the diffusion model can use thousands of kilowatt-hours, and refining it with FL across a constellation adds even more, which affects sustainability and the carbon budget for 6G [214]. In practice, NTN-SemCom deployments will need to spread this training energy over the mission lifetime.

VIII-C On-Board Model Compression and Deployment

Most published SemCom systems implicitly assume a deep encoder at the transmitter and a deep decoder at the receiver, with both ends free to host large models. However, this assumption tragically fails for NTNs, where the transmitter can be either a satellite or a UAV, and is still bounded by size, weight, power, and hardware constraints. Specifically, the large models’ demand not only for higher energy consumption but also for larger hardware deployments, which can consume more energy during hovering. On the other hand, the ground gateway can access unlimited energy and computing hardware, which facilitates large-model deployments. This asymmetry is widely acknowledged but often overlooked in current studies. One promising solution to address this issue is to adopt an asymmetry encoder-decoder architecture design [215], where the encoder at NTN devices can be lightweight designed following various efficient models: quantized, pruned, or even knowledge distilled from a larger model, paired with a high computing decoder, such as a foundation model. For instance, the satellite extracted the semantic features as knowledge graphs, which can be synthesized into high-quality images by a condition diffusion model [216]. The second challenge is the hardware that the encoder actually has to run on, the processors used in space are far behind ordinary ground GPUs- by roughly ten to fifteen years- because they must be built to survive radiation[217]. As a result, an encoder that runs easily on the ground may be too heavy to run in orbit at all.

VIII-D Standardization and Compatibility with 3GPP NTN

Regardless of the technical merits, SemCom is required to reconcile with the 3GPP standardization roadmap before being deployed in commercial NTN. However, the roadmap is itself moving toward the SemCom, where Release 17 introduced NTN with transparent payloads, Release 18 enhanced timing and HARQ to cope with long delays, and Release 20 is expected to embed AI/ML-native designs and intersect more strongly with sensing. To be included in the standardization mainstream, three main questions need to be answered: 1) Can SemCom be introduced as an application-layer service running on top of new radio waveforms? 2) Can a standard measurement/metric be established and widely accepted? 3) Can the SemCom-aware receiver and bit-level one share the time-frequency resources, which indicate the possible coexistence without any interruption to the other? Resolving these questions can lead to the standardization of SemCom in 3GPP.

VIII-E Channel-Adaptive Coding under High-Doppler and Time-Varying SNR

The channel-adaptive SemCom was examined in Section V-B, where they assume the channel is short-term stationary so that the coding decision made now remains valid for the next several symbols. In contrast, the LEO links frequently violate this assumption, whose SNR can fall by 5 dB within seconds, and the Doppler shift evolves continuously. This means a system that simply reacts to whatever the channel looks like right now will always be one step behind, because by the time it adjusts coding rates and strategy, the channel has already changed dramatically. The first mechanism to address this issue is to predict and pre-compensate the expected SNR and Doppler evolution over the visibility window rather than react to the measured values. The second approach is to leverage knowledge of the satellite’s precise orbital motion and schedule the transmission of the most important feature in advance, when the link is strongest. The third approach to revisit the feedback solution, where conventional HARQ fails in NTN due to long round-trip delays. However, semantic feedback is far more compact, and the receiver only requires the missing semantic symbol rather than the complete message.

VIII-F Shared Model Maintenance

SemCom systems rely on the common understanding between the transmitter and receiver, where this common understanding depends on the paradigm. In D-JSCC, the shared asset is gradually accumulated throughout the end-to-end training process. In generative AI and Theory-of-mind SemCom, the shared asset is normally a KB, a generative model, or a structured set of facts that the receiver uses to reconstruct or reason about meaning. All of SemCom’s work can only function properly when shared knowledge is synchronized among the communicating parties. In a heterogeneous NTNs of thousands of devices spanning multiple orbits, vendors, and firmware versions, maintaining the shared knowledge is a system-level problem. Three open questions for this matter can be presented as: How can a newly launched satellite obtain this shared knowledge? How can the updates propagate across the fleet without flooding already scarce links? And finally, when a mismatch happens, how can we detect and handle it?

VIII-G Threats, defense, and AI Safety of SemCom under NTNs

SemCom inherits the security risks of DL models and adds new risks because it protects meaning. We group the discussion into three parts: general threats that apply to any SemCom link, extra risks caused by NTN, and the defenses.

VIII-G1 General Threats

The first is eavesdropping on semantic features, where a passive attacker listens to the wireless signal and tries to recover the source data or task labels using a stolen or fake decoder. Since a semantic stream carries compact meaning, a successful attack can reveal more useful information than a normal bit stream. A mission-oriented secure semantic satellite communication method [210] addresses this by using a weighted fractional Fourier transform, where the transform order acts as a shared key, making eavesdropping much harder under realistic LEO multipath while keeping legitimate reception unchanged. The second threat is adversarial perturbation of the encoder or decoder: an attacker makes small, carefully designed changes to the input or to the transmitted symbols so that the receiver gives a wrong task result [218]. The main defense is adversarial training, and paired adversarial residual networks [211] have also been proposed for security-aware SemCom. The third threat targets the shared knowledge base through model-inversion or membership-inference attacks, an attacker with access to an FL-updated knowledge base may try to recover training data or check whether a sample was used during training. Differential privacy and gradient encryption can reduce these risks, but usually at some cost in accuracy. In short, these three threats affect message confidentiality, inference integrity, and knowledge-base privacy.

VIII-G2 The extreme of these threats in NTNs

These threats become even more serious in NTNs, where a multi-hop relay network introduces a risk of compromised relays: a malicious relay node can subtly alter the semantic features it forwards. This attack can be extremely hard to detect at the destination, and the final task result becomes biased. Due to the nature of the multi-hop setting, identifying the source of the attack is challenging. The work [22] indicated practical defenses to such problems are still underdeveloped. The multi-operator structure can create a long-baseline trust problem, where satellites, HAPS, UAVs, and a gateway are normally operated by different companies, and there is a demand to agree on a shared knowledge base, which becomes much more challenging. In addition, the long signal delays in NTN pose an ordinary challenge: response authentication is far too slow. This calls for lightweight, delay-tolerant ways to establish trust, such as threshold cryptography or pre-distributed semantic anchors. Finally, the broadcast geometry creates a jamming asymmetry. A ground-based attacker can disrupt the user-facing downlink with only modest power, and the damage is greater since a heavily compressed semantic stream has very little of the built-in redundancy that helps a bit-level stream survive sudden interference. In short, each NTN-specific concern is a familiar security threat amplified by a structural property of its own architecture.

VIII-G3 The potential solution against threats in SemCom-assisted NTN

The first strengthens the learned model itself through adversarial training across the channel, training the encoder, decoder, and channel together rather than separately. This makes the whole system robust to both semantic perturbation and channel noise [219, 220]. The second approach turns the wireless medium from a weakness into a defense. Physical-layer-secure SemCom uses the channel itself. For example, it uses friendly jamming at known eavesdropper locations [221, 222], beamforming and artificial-noise nulls directed at suspected attackers [223, 224], and encryption based on reciprocal channel measurements [225]. Spread-spectrum semantic encoders and frequency-hopping over codebook indices [117] also help address the earlier-mentioned jamming asymmetry. The third tackles the multi-operator trust problem directly through trust-bootstrapping mechanisms. These let satellites from different organizations share semantic context without exposing their private knowledge bases - for example, through hierarchical federated learning over LEO constellations [104], or blockchain-anchored multi-vendor federated training [226]. The important caveat is that none of these defenses has yet been tested under a single, complete threat model that captures the long delays, crowded spectrum, and multi-operator nature of a real NTN all at once. Such an end-to-end evaluation is one of the most urgent gaps in the literature.

VIII-G4 The safety of SemCom under NTN

Beyond these adversarial threats, there is a related set of concerns under the wider heading of AI safety. Since SemCom is built so closely on AI, it inherits AI’s weaknesses: hallucinations, adversarial attacks, privacy leakage, and knowledge mismatches between communicating agents. These issues matter most in safety-critical settings such as autonomous vehicles, UAV coordination, industrial automation, and satellite networks, where a single wrong interpretation can lead to a catastrophic decision. For example, if a generative decoder hallucinates a feature that does not exist in an Earth-observation image, it could trigger an unnecessary disaster response. Unlike eavesdropping or perturbation, this is not an attacker problem it is a reliability problem built into learned decoders. Promising fixes include measuring uncertainty in the decoder’s output, checking generated content against the symbolic rules of a knowledge graph, and adding abstention mechanisms that fall back to ordinary bit-level transmission when the decoder is not confident. Like the adversarial defenses above, testing these safeguards under realistic NTN conditions remains an open problem.

VIII-H Foundation Models, Quantum-Assisted SemCom, and the Internet of Space

This final challenge looks past small, near-term improvements toward the technologies that may reshape NTN-SemCom in the long run. Foundation models-large language models, multimodal vision-language models, and diffusion models-are already being used in satellite SemCom [93, 100, 107], but their use is still at an early stage. Three questions stand between today’s ad hoc use and a principled role. The first is universality: can one foundation model serve as the receiver for many different SemCom transmitters, acting as a single universal decoder so that each transmitter no longer needs to carry its own matched decoder? The second is the medium of communication between agents: in the Theory-of-Mind paradigm, agents exchange structured meaning, and LLMs may supply the shared, compact natural language in which that meaning is most efficiently expressed [11]. The third is placement: because of the SWaP-C asymmetry described before, it remains unclear when a billion-parameter model should be kept intact at a ground gateway and when it should be distilled into a much smaller model, on the order of a hundred million parameters, light enough to run on a HAPS or an LEO satellite. Together, these are the foundation model version of the deployment problem that recurs throughout this section. Foundation models, however, still assume that the link can carry a usable prompt. In deep space, this assumption breaks down: the links are so starved of photons that even a small foundation-model prompt may be too expensive to send, so a more radical solution is needed. Quantum semantic communication (QSC) has emerged to fill this gap, and in only a few years, it has moved from a speculative idea to a concrete research direction.

The conceptual groundwork was laid by Chehimi et al. [212]. Their first QSC framework maps classical data into high-dimensional quantum states using quantum machine learning, keeps only the semantic concepts that matter for the task, and sends them over quantum channels, reporting 50-75% resource savings compared with quantum networks that ignore semantics. Recent research has expanded both the uses and methods of QSC. Khalid et al. [227] applied QSC to metaverse services, using variational quantum computing and quantum anonymous communication to protect privacy. Rizvi et al. [228] developed controlled QSC for industrial cyber-physical systems by combining semantic extraction with controlled quantum-state preparation to securely detect anomalies. Nunavath et al. [229] applied knowledge-graph semantic encoders with variational quantum circuits. Raman et al. [230] argued that QSC is naturally resilient because the no-cloning theorem prevents an eavesdropper from copying a quantum-encoded semantic state without being detected.

The most significant recent progress is experimental. Wang et al. [213] reported the first experimental QSC demonstration, sending 3D point clouds over 50 km of optical fiber with a reported 46.30×\times efficiency gain over direct quantum transmission, which should be interpreted with care. It is based on the amount of task-relevant information delivered, not on raw bits, so it does not exceed classical channel-capacity limits. Instead, it shows that the meaningful data is much smaller than the original source. For NTN, the outlook is promising because some of the required infrastructure is already in place. Satellite QKD links are operational [231, 232], and quantum federated learning frameworks for LEO constellations [233] offer a practical way to train these systems. The remaining challenges are physical rather than conceptual. These include limited photonic resources, the lack of space-qualified quantum memories, and the absence of mature hybrid classical-quantum protocols. All of these must be addressed before NTN-QSC can move from the lab to orbit.

Foundation models and quantum-assisted transmission represent two extremes of the link-budget spectrum, but both aim for the same goal. The Internet of Space vision [107] includes Earth observation, navigation, satellite-to-handset connections, deep-space exploration, and on-orbit servicing. Each of these has very different SemCom needs, ranging from real-time delivery to archival, delay-tolerant, and security-critical communication. Serving all of them requires a single framework in which SemCom encoders and decoders can be swapped, combined, and updated across the whole ecosystem, rather than being rebuilt for every mission. Building such a framework is a long-term goal, and the recurring threads of standardization, foundation models, and federated learning are the most likely building blocks from which it will be assembled.

IX Conclusion

This survey has offered a comprehensive review of semantic communication in non-terrestrial networks. We began with the fundamentals, covering NTN architecture alongside the three primary SemCom approaches: D-JSCC, generative AI, and knowledge-graph/Theory-of-Mind methods. We then worked through each of the key NTN challenges in turn: severe path loss, long delays, Doppler shifts, intermittent connectivity, atmospheric effects, on-board hardware limits, multi-hop distortion and showed how specific SemCom techniques can turn each obstacle into an opportunity for better design. With a four-layer architecture and a three-part taxonomy in place, we examined satellite-focused SemCom in depth, spanning Earth observation, adaptive coding, generative AI, multi-hop routing, resource management, and federated learning. The discussion then moved to UAV and HAPS SemCom, including D-JSCC for image transmission, cognitive systems built on knowledge graphs, joint trajectory and resource planning, and federated learning. For integrated SAGIN/SAGSIN systems, we looked at architectural visions, multi-tier relays, probabilistic SemCom, and generative AI. Finally, we drew together eight key open challenges and pointed to the directions we see as most promising for future research. There are three main takeaways. First, the connection between SemCom and NTN is deliberate: each challenge in NTN has a matching SemCom feature that can help, and this relationship goes both ways. The demanding NTN environment encourages SemCom to become more adaptive, energy-efficient, distributed, and task-focused. These advances could also help future 6G networks on the ground. Second, progress is often slowed by hardware limits, gaps in knowledge-base infrastructure, or missing standards, rather than by a lack of algorithms. Third, the hardest problems are in the satellite layer, while UAV issues are usually easier to address and HAPS remains mostly unexplored. As 6G standards develop and large satellite constellations become more common, semantic communication is set to grow from a group of specialized codecs into a core principle for all non-terrestrial networks. Achieving this will rely more on systems-level progress, such as practical on-board encoders, shared and trusted knowledge bases, and standardized semantic protocols and benchmarks. Foundation-model and quantum-assisted SemCom will be the core technology for the Internet of Space.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
